_comment: 内置知识库的英文文案（i18n L3）。前端在英文界面请求扫描/概览/子目录等接口时带 lang=en，后端在响应出口按 rule_id 用这里的文本覆盖 what/advice/tip 与置信度标签。缺键即回落中文 —— 只影响显示，不参与任何判定。rules 里收三类 id：filetypes.json 的规则 id、app.py 内联分支的伪 id（steam-game / epic-game / gog-game / other-game-lib，由 mk() 写入 rule_id）、以及资源包条目 id（packs_lookup 对未识别节点写 rule_id=<包id>:<条目id>；advice 对应包内 effect+keep 的合并，tip 对应 rebuild）。

steam-library.what: Steam's game installation library: each subfolder is usually one game, plus appmanifest_*.acf files that record install state.
steam-library.advice: Do not delete files here. Uninstall games from the Steam client instead, otherwise you leave broken install records behind.
steam-library.tip: To reclaim space, sort your Steam library by size (Installed → Sort by size) and find the big games you no longer play.

game-generic.what: A folder that, by name, stores games or game platforms. Game installs are usually the single largest items on this machine.
game-generic.advice: Not recommended for bulk cleanup. What can usually be cleaned inside: installers, logs, crash dumps, and old update packages.
game-generic.tip: Subfolders named install / setup / patch / backup can usually be rebuilt by the launcher's 'verify files' feature.

emulator.what: Android emulator program and its virtual machine images. Images (.vdi/.vmdk) easily reach tens of GB and contain the apps and data you installed inside the emulator.
emulator.advice: Do not delete directly. To reclaim space, remove unused instances in the emulator's multi-instance manager / disk cleanup, or uninstall the whole emulator.
emulator.tip: Emulators often leave leftovers behind — watch for stray image files elsewhere.

gopro-exports.what: GoPro camera footage or exported edits. 4K/5K video runs hundreds of MB per minute, so these folders easily reach tens of GB.
gopro-exports.advice: Irreplaceable personal footage — the last thing you should clean. Archive to an external drive or cloud storage first, verify, then delete the local copy.
gopro-exports.tip: Archive the raw footage first; for finished edits you may only need the final cut.

video-media.what: A folder holding movies, TV shows, or recordings — the fastest-growing category of disk usage.
video-media.advice: Personal data; deleting it is unrecoverable. Decide yourself which items you have watched and no longer need.
video-media.tip: This tool never suggests cleaning such folders on its own; it only shows you the usage.

photo-cloud.what: Local sync folder of a photo library or cloud drive; files are usually already — or currently being — synced to the cloud.
photo-cloud.advice: Do not delete local files directly — some cloud drives sync deletions to the cloud. Use the client's 'online-only / free up space' feature instead.
photo-cloud.tip: After confirming a complete cloud copy exists, set files to 'online-only' in the client rather than deleting them.

download-dir.what: Default download location of a browser or download tool. Download folders mix uninstalled software, documents you want to keep, and other files — names alone cannot tell which are still needed. An external security audit (2026-10) confirmed that 'treat every download folder as cleanable' is a high-risk design that leads to accidental deletion, so this tool now defaults to keep.
download-dir.advice: Open the folder and look through it yourself: redundant .exe/.msi installers, .iso images, and unfinished .part files can go; documents, photos, and project files should not. When cleaning, select items manually in the usage list (the UI asks for a second confirmation).
download-dir.tip: Cleaning a download folder by name alone is a capability this tool deliberately removed — deleted downloads usually have no second copy.

chat-cache.what: Data folder of chat apps such as WeChat / QQ / Telegram: chat history, received images and videos, voice caches. Growing to tens of GB is common.
chat-cache.advice: Do not delete the folder itself — you would lose chat history. Use the client instead: Settings → Storage, and clean by conversation or by date.
chat-cache.tip: Telegram's media cache has copies in the cloud, so clearing it is safer than for WeChat; for WeChat use the in-app cleaner to avoid index corruption.

cloud-disk.what: Local data folder of a cloud-drive client: caches, streamed-video caches, and transfer files. Sync drives such as OneDrive fall into this category too.
cloud-disk.advice: Playback caches and transfer files can be cleaned (originals are in the cloud). Do not delete files of a sync drive directly — the deletion syncs to the cloud.
cloud-disk.tip: Once you cancel an unfinished transfer, its chunk files can be cleaned.

editing-project.what: Project folder of a video editor or other creative software. Besides project files it usually holds large preview/render caches (proxy/preview/cache).
editing-project.advice: Do not delete the folder as a whole. Only cache / preview / proxy subfolders may be cleaned; the project files themselves must stay.
editing-project.tip: Jianying (CapCut CN) drafts live under AppData\Local\JianyingPro; exported videos usually land elsewhere.

photoshop.what: Data folder of Adobe software: scratch files, Camera Raw cache, preview caches, and possibly your artwork project files.
photoshop.advice: Scratch and cache folders can be cleaned. Do not delete project files (.psd/.psb/.tif) or source assets.
photoshop.tip: Photoshop's scratch can grow to tens of GB with large images; it is released automatically when you close PS.

office-tools.what: Data folder of Office deployment tools (e.g. Office Tool Plus) or WPS. The former caches Office installation sources (several GB); the latter holds a backup center and cloud-document caches.
office-tools.advice: Keep the programs themselves. Installation-source caches and cloud-document caches can be cleaned; WPS's backup center may hold historical versions of your documents — confirm before deleting.
office-tools.tip: WPSDrive and the backup center often keep older versions of important documents; do not treat them as junk.

browser-data.what: Browser data folder in a non-default location (portable or custom install). It holds both caches (deletable) and bookmarks, passwords, cookies, sessions, and extensions (not deletable).
browser-data.advice: Do not delete the folder as a whole — you would lose bookmarks, passwords, and every login session. This tool splits it up for you: only cache subfolders such as Cache / Code Cache / GPUCache are listed as cleanable; the rest is marked keep.
browser-data.tip: Expand this item to see which subfolders can go and which must stay. The 'Chrome/Edge web cache' entry in the main list is the easier way to clear caches.

game-launcher.what: Game launcher folder with version libraries, dependency files, and download caches. Minecraft's version library alone often reaches several GB.
game-launcher.advice: Download caches and old versions you no longer play can be cleaned; keep saves and versions you are actively playing.
game-launcher.tip: After deleting old versions, the launcher re-downloads them on demand.

music-app.what: Cache and download folder of a music app: preview caches, downloaded songs, lyrics and cover art.
music-app.advice: Cache folders can be cleaned. Keep downloaded songs if you still want offline listening; deleting them means re-downloading.
music-app.tip: Many music apps store downloads in an encrypted format playable only inside their own client.

model-weights.what: Weights of local LLM / image-generation models, several GB to tens of GB each, and slow to download.
model-weights.advice: This is 'delete it and you re-download it' data. Unused models can be removed to save space, but make sure you no longer need them.
model-weights.tip: The classic trade-off: big space savings, paid back in re-download time. Whether to clean depends entirely on whether you still use the model.

docker-vm.what: Docker images, WSL distro disks, or VM disk files — commonly tens of GB each, and they keep growing with use.
docker-vm.advice: Do not delete the files directly; that corrupts images. For Docker use docker system prune; for WSL use wsl --unregister; remove VMs from within their software.
docker-vm.tip: These virtual disks never shrink automatically, even after you delete files inside them.

software-dir.what: By name, a folder where you centralize software — either installed programs or a collection of installers.
software-dir.advice: First tell apart 'installed programs' from 'installer archives': the former must be uninstalled properly; old versions of the latter can be cleaned.
software-dir.tip: Expand and look: folders containing .exe and dll files should not be touched; folders holding only versioned installers are usually archives.

drivers.what: Download cache of driver-manager software (Driver Genius and the like) or a driver backup folder you created yourself. Once drivers are installed, these packages are no longer needed.
drivers.advice: Cleanable, but keep the most recent working GPU/network-driver backup so you can roll back if something breaks.
drivers.tip: Old driver packages with dates or version numbers are safe to delete; keep only the latest. A bare 'driver/drivers' name is no longer used as evidence by itself — GPU driver packages and programs' own drivers folders share the name, and deleting the wrong one causes trouble.

windows-update-cache.what: Windows Update download caches, peer-distribution caches, or old-system files kept by a feature update for rollback. Can reach 10-30 GB.
windows-update-cache.advice: Cleanable. Once upgrade leftovers are removed you cannot roll back to the previous version — wait until the system has run stably for a while.
windows-update-cache.tip: The proper way is Settings → System → Storage → Cleanup recommendations; do not delete by hand.

game-shadercache.what: Shader pre-compilation cache generated by the game itself, inside the game's install folder.
game-shadercache.advice: Cleanable and reclaims space. The game's next launch will be slightly slower (the cache rebuilds), then back to normal.
game-shadercache.tip: These folders commonly grow to several GB — 'delete for real savings, the cost is one slow launch'.

cache-temp.what: By name, a cache or temporary-files folder; contents can generally be deleted and regenerated by the program.
cache-temp.advice: Cleanable. Files currently in use are skipped automatically.
cache-temp.tip: After cleanup, affected programs may start slightly slower the first time (caches rebuild).

logs-dumps.what: Program runtime logs or crash-time memory dumps. Useless for daily use; useful only while debugging a problem.
logs-dumps.advice: Usually cleanable. If you are currently debugging a program's issue, keep those for now.
logs-dumps.tip: Some misbehaving programs write tens of GB of logs — worth checking first.

node-modules.what: npm project dependencies. A single project easily takes hundreds of MB, and several projects add up fast.
node-modules.advice: Deletable; run npm install in the project to fully restore it later. Ideal cleanup target for unmaintained old projects.
node-modules.tip: Do not delete for projects still in development — reinstalling dependencies takes time and needs a network connection.

python-env.what: Python virtual environments, Conda environments, or bytecode caches. Each environment contains all third-party packages installed into it.
python-env.advice: Old unused environments can be deleted; rebuilding means reinstalling dependencies. __pycache__ is pure cache — delete freely.
python-env.tip: The pkgs folder inside a Conda installation is a download cache and can be cleaned on its own.

recycle-bin.what: This drive's Recycle Bin: files already deleted once. Emptying it is unrecoverable.
recycle-bin.advice: Make sure nothing inside is still needed, then empty it. The main list has a dedicated Recycle Bin entry that lists large items one by one.
recycle-bin.tip: Every drive has its own Recycle Bin; deleted files go to the bin of the drive they lived on.

system-volume.what: System restore points, shadow copies, file history — system-level snapshots. Usage depends on how much space you allotted to restore.
system-volume.advice: Do not delete manually (it fails on permissions anyway). Configure it under System Properties → System Protection.
system-volume.tip: If this folder is unusually large, the restore-point space cap is probably set high.

backup-dir.what: Backup files — system backups, automatic software backups, or backups you placed here yourself.
backup-dir.advice: Before deleting, confirm the data exists elsewhere. Clean only clearly outdated old backups and keep at least the most recent one.
backup-dir.tip: For rolling automatic backups, keeping the latest 1-2 copies is usually enough.

game-exe.what: A game's main executable or launcher. Such .exe files live inside the game's install folder; deleting one breaks the game.
game-exe.advice: Do not delete. Uninstall games via Steam / Epic / the launcher — the client cleans everything up properly.
game-exe.tip: How to tell: it sits in the game's common folder, not in a download folder — the same-named file in a download folder is just an installer.

game-data-pack.what: Game resource data packs (Rockstar .rpf, EA .big/.bdt, Valve .vpk, etc.). These ARE the game's maps, textures, models, and audio — often several GB each.
game-data-pack.advice: Never delete them individually — one missing file and the game errors out or will not start. To reclaim space, uninstall the game through its launcher.
game-data-pack.tip: Names like levels_3.rpf or packs_1.rpf mean this is core game content.

pagefile.what: Windows virtual memory file. When physical RAM runs short the system swaps data here. Usually as large as, or larger than, your RAM.
pagefile.advice: Cannot be deleted; the system is using it (manual deletion fails). Resize it under Advanced system settings → Performance → Virtual memory, or move it to another drive.
pagefile.tip: This tool marks it non-cleanable and explains only.

hiberfil.what: File backing hibernation and Fast Startup, about 40%-100% of physical RAM, pre-allocated and held.
hiberfil.advice: Cannot be deleted directly. The only way to reclaim it is to turn hibernation off: run powercfg /h off as administrator (this also disables Fast Startup; powercfg /h on restores it).
hiberfil.tip: One of the most common 'single large files' on the system drive. This tool never runs powercfg for you, to avoid changing your startup experience.

installer-pkg.what: A software installer package. Once the software is installed, the package itself is usually no longer needed.
installer-pkg.advice: Usually cleanable. Confirm the software is installed, or that you no longer need the package.
installer-pkg.tip: Clean old installers with version numbers and dates first; keep the most recent one for reinstalls.

iso-image.what: Optical disc image or system image. System install images are commonly 4-6 GB; VM disks can be tens of GB.
iso-image.advice: After the system is installed, its image is usually cleanable. Do not delete VM disks (.vhd/.vhdx) directly — manage them from the VM software.
iso-image.tip: If the system image is already installed out, deleting it reclaims several GB.

archive.what: Compressed archive — could be a software distribution, asset pack, or backup. Big archives are invisible space hogs.
archive.advice: Archives you have already extracted and used are usually cleanable. If it is the only copy (e.g. a backup), confirm before deleting.
archive.tip: If the extracted folder still exists, the archive is generally redundant.

video-file.what: Video files — the fastest-growing disk usage category. A 4K movie over 20 GB is common.
video-file.advice: Personal data; deletion is unrecoverable. Decide yourself which ones you have watched and no longer need.
video-file.tip: This tool never suggests deleting videos; it shows the usage and lets you decide.

audio-file.what: Music or recording files. Lossless formats (.flac/.wav/.ape) can reach tens to hundreds of MB each.
audio-file.advice: Personal data. If it came from a music app, it can usually be re-downloaded there.
audio-file.tip: Locally recorded original audio is irreplaceable — be careful.

disk-image-backup.what: System or partition-level backup (Ghost, Acronis, etc.), commonly tens of GB each.
disk-image-backup.advice: Your lifeline when reinstalling the system — not recommended to delete. If a newer backup exists, the old one can go.
disk-image-backup.tip: Delete an old backup only after confirming the newer one actually restores.

ai-weights.what: LLM or image-model weight files, commonly 2-40 GB each.
ai-weights.advice: Deleting means re-downloading (slow and data-hungry). Unused models can be removed.
ai-weights.tip: The test is simple: do you still use this model?

game-asset.what: Game engine asset packs (Unreal .pak/.ucas/.utoc, etc.). These ARE the game's art and audio resources.
game-asset.advice: Never delete them individually — one missing file and the game fails to start or crashes constantly. To reclaim space, uninstall the game through its launcher.
game-asset.tip: Names like pakchunk10-WindowsClient.ucas mean this is core content of an Unreal Engine game.

log-dump-file.what: Program logs or crash dumps; useful only while debugging.
log-dump-file.advice: Usually cleanable. Keep them if you are currently troubleshooting a failure.
log-dump-file.tip: Some misbehaving programs write tens of GB of logs.

office-doc.what: Office documents or design source files. Shown so you can see where space goes — not a suggestion to delete.
office-doc.advice: Personal data; decide yourself. Back up important documents elsewhere regularly.
office-doc.tip: This tool never lists documents as cleanup suggestions.

steam-game.what: Steam game install: this folder is the entire game.
steam-game.advice: Games you no longer play can be deleted whole, reclaiming several GB to 100+ GB at once. Prefer uninstalling in the Steam client (right-click the game → Manage → Uninstall), which also clears the library record; deleting the folder works too — Steam then shows it as 'not installed' and you can re-download anytime. Note: a few games keep saves, configs, or mods in the install folder (most keep saves in Documents\My Games, AppData, or Steam Cloud) — check before deleting.

epic-game.what: Game installed by the Epic Games launcher: this folder is the entire game.
epic-game.advice: Games you no longer play can be deleted whole. Prefer removing them in Epic (Settings → Manage) which cleans the records too; deleting the folder directly also frees the space. Note: GOG/older games often keep saves in the install folder or Documents\My Games — confirm no saves you want to keep.

gog-game.what: Game installed by GOG: this folder is the entire game.
gog-game.advice: Games you no longer play can be deleted whole. Prefer uninstalling via GOG Galaxy, which also cleans registry records; deleting the folder directly also frees the space. Note: GOG/older games often keep saves in the install folder or Documents\My Games — confirm no saves you want to keep.

other-game-lib.what: Epic/GOG game library folder; each subfolder is one game's installation.

explanations:exp-cache-temp.what: Temporary data produced while programs run: half-downloaded update packages, intermediate files from extractions, and cached copies kept to open things faster next time. Programs are designed assuming these files can disappear at any moment.
explanations:exp-cache-temp.advice: A few programs open slightly slower the first time afterwards (caches rebuild), and programs currently running may show brief loading errors — so close the related program before cleaning. If you keep your own files in such folders (some people use temp as a staging area), look before deleting.
explanations:exp-cache-temp.tip: Regenerates automatically, usually on demand the next time you use the related feature.

explanations:exp-logs-dumps.what: Running logs written by programs and the 'crash scene photos' taken when something fails (crash dumps). Logs are for troubleshooting; dumps are for analyzing why a program crashed.
explanations:exp-logs-dumps.advice: After deletion, evidence of past problems is gone: if a recent software issue is still unresolved or you need to send diagnostics to a developer, keep them for a few more days. When nothing is being investigated, it is safe to clean.
explanations:exp-logs-dumps.tip: New ones keep appearing as programs continue to run.

explanations:exp-win-update-cache.what: Installers downloaded by Windows Update, staging files from upgrades, and Windows.old — the old system kept after a feature upgrade for rollback.
explanations:exp-win-update-cache.advice: Once Windows.old is removed you can no longer roll back to the previous version; if an update cache is cleared mid-update, the update must re-download. Nothing else is affected. Right after a feature upgrade, keep Windows.old until the new system is confirmed fine (Windows removes it itself after 10 days).
explanations:exp-win-update-cache.tip: Re-downloaded the next time an update needs it.

explanations:exp-shadercache.what: Cache of compiled rendering instructions kept by the GPU driver or games, avoiding recompilation on every launch — recompiling is the stutter and the shader-compilation progress bar you see.
explanations:exp-shadercache.advice: The first few launches after cleaning load slower and may stutter in places; things return to normal after a few sessions. Not worth cleaning for games you play often — the benefit is momentary; it is a safe candidate when the disk is full and you need space.
explanations:exp-shadercache.tip: Rebuilt automatically the next time you launch the game.

explanations:exp-node-modules.what: Third-party dependency packages of JavaScript projects. One copy per project, easily hundreds of MB — the main disk consumer of frontend/Node projects.
explanations:exp-node-modules.advice: The project cannot run or build until dependencies are reinstalled. Delete them only in old unmaintained projects — doing it to active projects just creates work for yourself. Leave them alone while a project is in active development.
explanations:exp-node-modules.tip: Run `npm install` in the project (or the pnpm/yarn equivalent) to fully restore from package.json.

explanations:exp-python-env.what: venv is a project's isolated Python environment (including its installed libraries); conda/anaconda/miniconda are the distribution itself or its package caches; __pycache__ is bytecode cache.
explanations:exp-python-env.advice: After deleting a venv, the project needs its environment rebuilt to run; deleting the conda/anaconda folder itself also removes every environment installed inside it — make sure it is a cache folder before deleting. If you cannot tell a venv from the conda installation itself, do not delete large folders named conda/anaconda.
explanations:exp-python-env.tip: __pycache__ regenerates automatically; a deleted venv must be rebuilt from requirements.txt; deleting the conda installation equals uninstalling the distribution.

explanations:exp-recycle-bin.what: The staging area for files you (and other programs) deleted. Emptying it is the final, unrecoverable delete.
explanations:exp-recycle-bin.advice: After emptying, the contents are truly gone — no tool can bring them back. Review the contents before emptying, and hold off if you recently deleted something you might want to restore.
explanations:exp-recycle-bin.tip: The system folder structure rebuilds automatically.

explanations:exp-download-dir.what: Where browsers and download tools save files. These are your own files — installed-out installers, documents you received, saved images and videos.
explanations:exp-download-dir.advice: Useless installers are fair game to delete; but the folder often also holds the only copy of documents, invoices, or files shared via chat — review item by item rather than wiping the whole folder in one go. Move anything uncertain elsewhere first; installers you can re-download anytime are the safest things to clean here.
explanations:exp-download-dir.tip: Nothing regenerates — once deleted, it is gone.

explanations:exp-cloud-disk.what: Caches and sync data of cloud-drive clients. Note the difference: clearing caches is harmless, but the client's 'sync folder' may hold the only local copy of your cloud files.
explanations:exp-cloud-disk.advice: After clearing caches, previously cached files must be fetched from the network again. If you cannot tell cache folders from sync folders, clean only the one whose name contains cache.
explanations:exp-cloud-disk.tip: Caches rebuild; a deleted sync-folder copy is gone locally but still in the cloud (unless what you deleted was the cloud's sync source).

explanations:exp-installer-pkg.what: Software installers. Usually useless once installed, but they are the only proof of where this particular download came from.
explanations:exp-installer-pkg.advice: Reinstalling the same version means finding the installer again; installed, working software is not affected. Offline installers of frequently used software and internally distributed corporate installers are worth keeping — they take little space.
explanations:exp-installer-pkg.tip: Official sites and app stores always have fresh downloads, but old versions, niche software, and offline installers may be impossible to find again.

explanations:exp-iso-image.what: Whole-disc/system images (.iso/.wim/.esd) or virtual machine disk files (.vhd/.vhdx).
explanations:exp-iso-image.advice: Deleting a .vhd/.vhdx equals deleting everything in that virtual machine; deleting a system image only loses a ready-made reinstall medium. First confirm ownership: VM disks stay, always; images you can re-download online are deletable.
explanations:exp-iso-image.tip: Nothing regenerates — a system image must be rebuilt, and a VM disk holds your entire installed system.

explanations:exp-archive.what: Compressed archives: downloaded resources, collections shared by others, or your own archived old files.
explanations:exp-archive.advice: If it was 'extract once, then useless' it can go; if the archive itself is the asset (never extracted, or the extracted copy was already deleted), deleting it loses it for good. If you already keep the contents as normal files, the archive can go; otherwise open and confirm first.

explanations:exp-log-dump-file.what: Individual log or crash-dump files, mostly scattered around. Text logs are usually tiny; dumps can reach tens to hundreds of MB.
explanations:exp-log-dump-file.advice: You lose the evidence for troubleshooting past problems; nothing else is affected. Clean when nothing is being investigated; if logs must go to technical support, send them first.
explanations:exp-log-dump-file.tip: Programs keep writing new ones as they run.

explanations:exp-drivers.what: Driver packages downloaded by driver-manager tools, or drivers you backed up manually. They are installers — deleting them does not affect the drivers already installed.
explanations:exp-drivers.advice: After deletion, an offline system reinstall has no driver packages on hand and you must find them online on the spot. Keep a set if you regularly install systems on old or offline machines; otherwise clean.
explanations:exp-drivers.tip: Re-downloadable via driver tools or the hardware vendor's website when needed.

explanations:exp-music-app.what: Music app caches and downloaded songs. Caches are temporary listening data; the downloads folder may hold local files of your subscription songs.
explanations:exp-music-app.advice: Caches re-buffer after cleaning; songs in the downloads folder must be re-downloaded, and on some platforms offline songs stop working. Tell the cache and downloads subfolders apart — the latter are songs you chose; think before deleting.

explanations:exp-photoshop.what: Caches, presets, and data of the Adobe suite. Media caches (preview indexes of video editors) can be cleaned; preset, action, and plug-in folders must not be touched.
explanations:exp-photoshop.advice: After clearing media caches, reopening a project regenerates previews; deleting the wrong presets or plug-ins folder loses your custom configuration. Only clean subfolders whose names say cache / media cache; never touch project files and preset folders.
explanations:exp-photoshop.tip: Media caches rebuild when the project is reopened.

explanations:exp-office-tools.what: Office deployment tool install caches and WPS caches/configuration. Caches can be cleaned; WPS folders may also hold local copies of cloud documents and custom templates.
explanations:exp-office-tools.advice: After clearing caches and downloaded install sources, a repair install re-downloads; deleting the config folder loses templates and settings. Do not touch anything marked local backup or cloud document copy.

explanations:exp-game-launcher.what: Version libraries and resource caches of Minecraft launchers (PCL/HMCL etc.) and download caches of various game launchers. Minecraft keeps a full copy per version, and old versions pile up.
explanations:exp-game-launcher.advice: Deleting versions you no longer play is harmless; deleting a version you play means re-downloading the whole pack, and launcher configuration (save paths, Java settings) may go with it. Confirm which versions are still being played; never delete saves (the saves folder).

explanations:exp-im-chat.what: Local data of chat apps like WeChat/QQ: chat history databases, files, images, and videos sent in chats, plus huge image/video caches. Caches dominate, but the folder mixes in the chat history itself.
explanations:exp-im-chat.advice: After clearing caches, images and videos in chats reload from the cloud (expired content may no longer load); deleting the data folder wipes this machine's chat history to zero. Clean only subfolders like cache or year-month folders under FileStorage; never bulk-delete the whole data folder. If chat history matters, back it up with the app's own backup feature first.
explanations:exp-im-chat.tip: Caches rebuild; chat history does not — once deleted it is gone (unless you had backup or roaming enabled).

explanations:exp-video-edit.what: Draft projects and asset caches of video editors like Jianying. Draft folders hold unexported editing projects (timelines, subtitles, transition settings); caches are preview copies of assets.
explanations:exp-video-edit.advice: After clearing caches, completed projects must re-link assets when reopened; deleting the drafts folder makes unexported work vanish immediately. Export-and-backup any unexported project before touching anything; if you cannot tell drafts from caches, leave the whole folder alone.

explanations:exp-torrent.what: BT client task data: in-flight chunks, seeding tasks, and tracker/verification caches. Note that completed downloads usually live in a separate folder you chose, not here.
explanations:exp-torrent.advice: Deleting cancels unfinished downloads and removes seeding tasks; completed files are unaffected (unless the save folder is set here too). Do not clean while seeding or sharing tasks exist; pure caches and leftover chunks are safe to clean.
explanations:exp-torrent.tip: Reinstalling the client does not restore the task list; unfinished downloads cannot resume.

explanations:exp-vm-dir.what: Where VMware / VirtualBox / Hyper-V virtual machines live: each subfolder is usually one complete VM (disk file + configuration + snapshots).
explanations:exp-vm-dir.advice: Deleting a subfolder deletes that VM entirely, snapshots included; remove only VMs you are certain are abandoned. Keep absolutely anything holding a unique environment (for example an old app that only runs in that VM); for abandoned VMs, prefer deleting from the client — cleaner than manual folder deletion.
explanations:exp-vm-dir.tip: Nothing regenerates — the disk file holds your entire installed system and data.

explanations:exp-ai-models.what: Local LLM data: models and dataset caches downloaded from HuggingFace, and model files pulled by Ollama / LM Studio. A single model is often several GB to tens of GB.
explanations:exp-ai-models.advice: Next use re-downloads everything; for Ollama prefer `ollama rm` over deleting the folder manually so its model list stays consistent. Keep frequently used models on offline or metered connections; deleting models you use daily is pure self-sabotage.
explanations:exp-ai-models.tip: Re-downloading restores them as-is (model files are public and version-pinned).

explanations:exp-dev-toolchain.what: Download caches and build intermediates of language package managers and build tools: pip wheel caches, npm/pnpm package caches, Gradle dependency and build caches, Cargo registry and build caches, and the Go build cache.
explanations:exp-dev-toolchain.advice: The first build after cleaning is noticeably slower (packages re-download from the network), then back to normal. Project sources and installed dependencies are never touched. For permanently offline build environments, keeping caches saves a lot of downloading; on ordinary dev machines this is the safest first batch to clean.
explanations:exp-dev-toolchain.tip: Everything rebuilds on demand: dependencies re-download and builds recompile the next time.

games-platform:steam-common.what: Install location of all installed Steam games; each subfolder is one game.
games-platform:steam-common.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling, and Steam's installed record is not cleared with it; re-download to play again. Keep while you still want to play. To uninstall, use the Steam client's Manage → Uninstall so the record is cleared too.
games-platform:steam-common.tip: N/A: this is purchased, downloaded content; deleting means re-downloading.

games-platform:steam-downloading.what: Chunk files of games currently downloading or updating.
games-platform:steam-downloading.advice: After cleaning, the game must download from the beginning. Keep while a download task is in progress or you want to preserve its progress.
games-platform:steam-downloading.tip: Rebuilds automatically, but downloaded progress starts over.

games-platform:steam-temp.what: Temporary space used to unpack games during install or update.
games-platform:steam-temp.advice: Cleaning during an install breaks that install. No need to keep when no install task is running.

games-platform:steam-shadercache.what: Precompiled GPU shaders, reducing stutter on a game's first runs.
games-platform:steam-shadercache.advice: The first few runs after cleaning may stutter while compiling, then return to normal. No need to keep — and this is one of the larger categories; tens of GB is common.
games-platform:steam-shadercache.tip: Rebuilds automatically as the game runs.

games-platform:steam-workshop.what: Mods, maps, and other content subscribed from the Steam Workshop.
games-platform:steam-workshop.advice: After deletion, saves may fail to load for missing mods, or in-game items disappear. Keep them; to trim, unsubscribe in Steam and let the client handle it.

games-platform:steam-compatdata.what: The Windows-compatibility environment Proton / Steam Play prepares per game.
games-platform:steam-compatdata.advice: After deletion the game must re-initialize the compatibility environment; saves inside are lost with it. Keep them — most Windows users never need this.
games-platform:steam-compatdata.tip: Rebuilds automatically, but rebuilding takes a while.

games-platform:steam-appcache.what: UI caches, logs, and crash dumps of the Steam client.
games-platform:steam-appcache.advice: The client loads store pages slightly slower the first time after cleaning. No need to keep.

games-platform:steam-htmlcache.what: Web cache of the Steam client's built-in browser (store and community pages).
games-platform:steam-htmlcache.advice: After cleaning, community pages may ask you to verify again when re-logging in. No need to keep.

games-platform:steam-depotcache.what: Steam's manifest of downloaded content and chunk indexes.
games-platform:steam-depotcache.advice: After cleaning, Steam re-verifies installed games and may trigger a verification scan. No need to keep; keep it if you want to avoid the verification time.

games-platform:steam-userdata.what: Per-account local settings, local saves of some games, and cloud-sync staging files.
games-platform:steam-userdata.advice: Deleting may lose saves and settings not yet synced to the cloud. Keep.

games-platform:steam-libraryfolder.what: The location of one Steam library, containing steamapps and the games' install folders.
games-platform:steam-libraryfolder.advice: Deleting the whole thing uninstalls every game in this library. Keep.

games-platform:epic-games.what: Games installed through the Epic Games Launcher.
games-platform:epic-games.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling; Epic's installed record does not sync automatically, and leftover records can make the launcher error out before a reinstall. Keep them; use Epic's own uninstall feature to remove games.

games-platform:epic-launcher-cache.what: Logs, embedded web caches, and crash reports of the Epic launcher.
games-platform:epic-launcher-cache.advice: The launcher opens the store slightly slower the first time after cleaning. No need to keep.

games-platform:epic-launcher-data.what: Login credentials, installed-game manifests, and settings.
games-platform:epic-launcher-data.advice: After deletion you must log in again, and the launcher loses its record of installed games. Keep.

games-platform:gog-games.what: Games installed through GOG Galaxy or offline installers.
games-platform:gog-games.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling. GOG saves often live inside the game folder and may be lost with it. Keep.
games-platform:gog-games.tip: N/A: re-download or reinstall to play again.

games-platform:gog-galaxy-cache.what: Logs and web caches of the GOG Galaxy client.
games-platform:gog-galaxy-cache.advice: The client opens slightly slower the first time after cleaning. No need to keep.

games-platform:game-saves-generic.what: Many games keep saves, configuration, and screenshots in these folders under Documents.
games-platform:game-saves-generic.advice: Deleting loses save progress. Some games have cloud saves, but not all, and syncing may lag. Always keep — this is a protect-list category this tool will not touch.

games-platform:game-shadercache-local.what: Shader compilation results generated by the GPU driver or the game itself, avoiding repeated compilation.
games-platform:game-shadercache-local.advice: The first few runs after cleaning may stutter, then recover. No need to keep.

games-platform:unreal-ddc.what: Unreal Engine's Derived Data Cache — cached material and shader compilation results, easily tens of GB.
games-platform:unreal-ddc.advice: Cleaning while a project is in progress makes the next compile noticeably slower. Developers who switch projects often save time by keeping it; as a pure player you can clean it. Note: in-progress projects may hold uncommitted intermediates here.
games-platform:unreal-ddc.tip: Rebuilds automatically, but the editor and games load very slowly while it does.

games-platform:unity-cache.what: Asset import caches and Asset Store download caches of the Unity editor.
games-platform:unity-cache.advice: The first project open after cleaning re-imports assets. Keep while a project is in progress to save time.

games-platform:game-anticheat-logs.what: Logs and run records of anti-cheat components.
games-platform:game-anticheat-logs.advice: Cleaning is usually harmless, but individual games may ask you to reinstall the anti-cheat component. If a game fails to launch over anti-cheat, keeping the logs helps troubleshooting.

windows-system:win-temp.what: System-level temp folder: installers, system components, and some software write intermediate files here.
windows-system:win-temp.advice: Files held by running programs cannot be deleted and are skipped; already-written but unused content may need to regenerate — a one-time time cost. Almost never worth keeping; if a system update or big install is running, clean after it finishes.
windows-system:win-temp.tip: Rebuilds on demand automatically; no manual intervention needed.

windows-system:win-prefetch.what: Windows' index of which files programs read at launch, used to speed up the next start.
windows-system:win-prefetch.advice: For a while after cleaning, frequently used programs may start slightly slower. Keep it if this machine has a mechanical disk and you care about launch speed; on SSDs the impact is tiny.
windows-system:win-prefetch.tip: Rebuilds automatically: after a few more launches the index is close to its original state.

windows-system:win-update-download.what: Update install packages already downloaded; useless once installed.
windows-system:win-update-download.advice: If an update is in the 'downloaded, pending install' state, cleaning means one more download. When the system says updates are waiting for a restart, install them before cleaning.

windows-system:win-delivery-optimization.what: Local cache of peer-to-peer distribution for Windows Update and Store apps, served to other devices on the LAN.
windows-system:win-delivery-optimization.advice: Cleaning itself is risk-free; it is also the 'upload to others' cache, so cleaning clears the record of uploaded share. No need to keep; if you care about upload traffic, turn it off under Settings → Windows Update → Delivery Optimization.

windows-system:win-logs.what: Run logs, setup logs, and troubleshooting records written by the system and components.
windows-system:win-logs.advice: If you happen to be debugging a failure, its logs are gone after cleaning. Keep them while investigating system problems; otherwise no need to keep.
windows-system:win-logs.tip: New logs keep being written as needed.

windows-system:win-minidump.what: Small memory images saved when the system blue-screens, for post-mortem crash analysis.
windows-system:win-minidump.advice: After cleaning you can no longer analyze that crash. Keep these files if the system has been blue-screening often recently.
windows-system:win-minidump.tip: Does not rebuild automatically; regenerated only at the next crash.

windows-system:win-livekernelreports.what: Diagnostic reports generated when the system detects anomalies at runtime; can be large.
windows-system:win-livekernelreports.advice: After cleaning you can no longer analyze that anomaly. No need to keep unless troubleshooting.
windows-system:win-livekernelreports.tip: Does not rebuild automatically; regenerated when a problem occurs.

windows-system:win-wer.what: Error reports and dump files collected after program crashes.
windows-system:win-wer.advice: After cleaning you can no longer analyze that crash. No need to keep unless troubleshooting.

windows-system:win-iedownloadedprogramfi.what: ActiveX component cache downloaded by legacy Internet Explorer; rarely used on modern Windows.
windows-system:win-iedownloadedprogramfi.advice: Intranet systems relying on legacy ActiveX may be affected. Keep only while legacy IE-kernel apps are still in use.

windows-system:win-inetcache.what: System-level HTTP cache, used by IE-kernel components and parts of the system UI.
windows-system:win-inetcache.advice: The first few accesses are slightly slower. No need to keep.

windows-system:win-thumbcache.what: The thumbnail database Explorer builds for images and videos, making folder previews faster.
windows-system:win-thumbcache.advice: The first open of an image-heavy folder regenerates thumbnails and is briefly slower. No need to keep. Note this folder also holds Explorer settings like window positions — this tool cleans only the cache files.
windows-system:win-thumbcache.tip: Rebuilds automatically as you browse the folders again.

windows-system:win-fontcache.what: Cache files the system generates to speed up font loading.
windows-system:win-fontcache.advice: Interfaces with lots of text may be slightly slower the first time. No need to keep; if deletion reports the file in use, clean again after a reboot.

windows-system:win-crashdumps.what: Memory dumps saved when ordinary programs crash; a single file can reach hundreds of MB.
windows-system:win-crashdumps.advice: After cleaning you can no longer analyze that crash. No need to keep unless debugging crashes.
windows-system:win-crashdumps.tip: Does not rebuild automatically; regenerated at the next crash.

windows-system:win-recycle-bin.what: Staging area for deleted files that can still be restored.
windows-system:win-recycle-bin.advice: After emptying, these files can no longer be brought back with Restore. Do not empty right after accidentally deleting something you plan to restore.
windows-system:win-recycle-bin.tip: N/A — this is a staging area for real files, not a cache.

windows-system:win-newsystemold.what: The complete previous Windows installation kept by a feature upgrade for rollback.
windows-system:win-newsystemold.advice: After deletion you cannot roll back to the pre-upgrade version, nor recover the old system's personal files from it. Keep it within 10 days of the upgrade or until the new system is confirmed fine; Windows cleans it up automatically when it expires.
windows-system:win-newsystemold.tip: N/A: this is a backup — once deleted, it is gone.

windows-system:win-hiberfil.what: The system writes RAM contents here when hibernating; usually close to the size of physical memory.
windows-system:win-hiberfil.advice: Deleting it directly does nothing — the system holds it open, and the next hibernation recreates it. The only way to reclaim the space is to turn hibernation off: run powercfg /h off as administrator. Keep it while you use hibernation or Fast Startup; disabling hibernation also disables Fast Startup.
windows-system:win-hiberfil.tip: It stays; it does not go away.

windows-system:win-pagefile.what: The swap files backing virtual memory, managed by the system.
windows-system:win-pagefile.advice: Deleting it gets the file rebuilt immediately — no space freed and stability may suffer. Always keep. Resize it under System Properties → Advanced → Performance → Virtual memory.

windows-system:win-installer.what: Cache of MSI packages and uninstall information for patches; many programs reference it when repairing, upgrading, or uninstalling.
windows-system:win-installer.advice: After cleaning you may see 'cannot uninstall', 'cannot repair', or 'upgrade failed', with the cause hard to track down. Keep it — this tool puts it on the protect list and never cleans it.

windows-system:win-winsxs.what: The component store holding side-by-side versions of system components; most of it is hard links, so real usage is far below the shown size.
windows-system:win-winsxs.advice: Manual deletion breaks system updating and component repair, and in bad cases the system will not boot. Keep it; to reclaim space use the official command DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /StartComponentCleanup.

windows-system:win-servicing.what: Staging area and component manifests for system updates.
windows-system:win-servicing.advice: Deletion can break updates or corrupt system components. Keep.

windows-system:win-csc.what: Local copies kept by the Offline Files feature for when network shares are unavailable.
windows-system:win-csc.advice: Deleting directly may lose changes not yet synced back to the server. Keep it; with Offline Files disabled it is basically empty.

windows-system:win-search-index.what: The index database Windows Search uses to match file contents quickly.
windows-system:win-search-index.advice: For a while after cleaning, search results are incomplete. Recommended to keep; to rebuild use Indexing Options → Advanced → Rebuild.
windows-system:win-search-index.tip: It rebuilds, but search is noticeably degraded during the rebuild and needs time to become complete again.

windows-system:win-uwp-packages.what: Per-app data, settings, and caches of each Store app (including some system components).
windows-system:win-uwp-packages.advice: Bulk deletion resets apps, requires re-login, and may upset individual system components. Keep it; clean per app instead — for example remove WSL distros with wsl --unregister.
windows-system:win-uwp-packages.tip: Some parts rebuild automatically, but app settings and login state are lost.

windows-system:win-speech-ime.what: Language resources used by speech recognition and input methods.
windows-system:win-speech-ime.advice: After cleaning, speech/typing for the affected language may be temporarily unavailable. Keep them; these folders are usually small.

windows-system:win-assembly.what: The .NET framework assembly cache; many older programs reference it at startup.
windows-system:win-assembly.advice: Deletion breaks programs that depend on .NET. Keep.

windows-system:win-security.what: System files related to security policy and credentials.
windows-system:win-security.advice: Deletion may affect login and permission checks. Keep.

windows-system:win-recovery.what: The system recovery environment plus temp folders left behind by upgrades.
windows-system:win-recovery.advice: $Windows.~BT / ~WS are upgrade leftovers, usually cleanable some time after the upgrade completes; \Recovery is the recovery environment — deleting it weakens system repair. Keep \Recovery; clean upgrade leftovers once the system is confirmed fine.

windows-system:win-setup-temp.what: Logs and temp files left by system installation and upgrades.
windows-system:win-setup-temp.advice: If an upgrade later fails, its setup logs are missing after cleaning. Keep them while an upgrade is in progress; clean after it completes and checks out.

apps-common:pip-cache.what: Cache of wheels and source packages downloaded by pip; installed libraries can be reused from it.
apps-common:pip-cache.advice: Reinstalling the same libraries re-downloads them after cleaning. Keep it on poor connections or when you re-create environments often.

apps-common:uv-cache.what: Package cache downloaded and built by uv.
apps-common:uv-cache.advice: First installs are slower after cleaning. No need to keep; use uv cache clean for a more proper cleanup when needed.

apps-common:npm-cache.what: Package cache downloaded by npm, often several GB.
apps-common:npm-cache.advice: Reinstalling dependencies re-downloads them after cleaning. Keep it when you often install dependencies offline.

apps-common:yarn-pnpm-store.what: Global package stores of yarn and pnpm; pnpm also hard-links from it to save space.
apps-common:yarn-pnpm-store.advice: After cleaning, every project's first dependency install is slower; pnpm's hard links break and re-fetch. The pnpm store is part of its space-saving mechanism — recommended to keep.

apps-common:gradle-caches.what: Dependencies downloaded by Gradle and its build caches.
apps-common:gradle-caches.advice: The first build after cleaning is noticeably slower; the wrapper may also hold the pinned Gradle distribution. Keep it when you build Android/Java projects often.
apps-common:gradle-caches.tip: Rebuilds, but dependencies re-download from the network.

apps-common:maven-repo.what: The local repository of jars downloaded by Maven.
apps-common:maven-repo.advice: Builds re-download dependencies after cleaning; offline builds fail outright. Keep it when you must build without network.

apps-common:nuget-packages.advice: Restoring dependencies re-downloads them after cleaning. Keep it when you build .NET projects often.

apps-common:go-modcache.what: Go module download cache and build intermediates; the build cache can reach tens of GB.
apps-common:go-modcache.advice: The first compile after cleaning starts from scratch and takes clearly longer. Keep it when compiling big projects frequently; go clean -cache is the more proper way.

apps-common:cargo-registry.what: Rust's crate download cache and copies of git dependencies.
apps-common:cargo-registry.advice: Builds re-download dependencies after cleaning. Keep it when you build Rust projects often.

apps-common:hf-cache.what: Model weights downloaded from Hugging Face; a single model is often tens of GB.
apps-common:hf-cache.advice: Deleting means re-downloading, and some models may have been taken down by their authors and cannot be fetched again. Recommended to keep — this is a protect-list category this tool will not touch.
apps-common:hf-cache.tip: It re-downloads, but at a high cost.

apps-common:ollama-models.advice: After deletion you must re-download and the same space is taken again. Keep them; to remove, use ollama rm <model>.
apps-common:ollama-models.tip: Can be re-pulled with ollama pull.

apps-common:torch-hub.advice: Deleting means re-downloading, possibly tens of GB. Keeping them is the easier path.

apps-common:wechat-files.what: Chat images, videos, files, and the chat history database saved by WeChat.
apps-common:wechat-files.advice: After deletion, local chat history and received files are unrecoverable, and expired content is no longer served by the servers. Always keep; slim it down with WeChat's own storage management. This tool never cleans it.
apps-common:wechat-files.tip: Does not rebuild automatically; servers usually keep content only for a limited time.

apps-common:wechat-cache.what: Cache data shared across WeChat accounts (stickers, thumbnails, etc.).
apps-common:wechat-cache.advice: Stickers and thumbnails reload after cleaning. No need to keep.

apps-common:qq-files.what: Files received by QQ, chat history, and images.
apps-common:qq-files.advice: Local history and files cannot be recovered after deletion. Keep; use QQ's own cleanup feature.

apps-common:telegram-tdata.what: Telegram's login state, session keys, and local caches.
apps-common:telegram-tdata.advice: After deletion you must log in again and receive a verification code on your phone. Keep it; to clear caches use Telegram's Settings → Advanced → Storage Usage.

apps-common:wecom-cache.what: Images, stickers, and temp files downloaded by workplace collaboration apps.
apps-common:wecom-cache.advice: Local copies of historical images and files disappear after cleaning and must be re-downloaded when needed. Confirm important files were saved elsewhere first.

apps-common:discord-cache.what: Caches of Discord's embedded browser, stickers, and images.
apps-common:discord-cache.advice: Channels reload their images the first time after cleaning. No need to keep.

apps-common:slack-teams-zoom-cache.what: Logs, caches, and temp files of these meeting and collaboration apps.
apps-common:slack-teams-zoom-cache.advice: First launch and loading history messages are slightly slower after cleaning. No need to keep.

apps-common:nvidia-shadercache.what: Shader caches compiled by the GPU driver for games and graphics software.
apps-common:nvidia-shadercache.advice: Games and graphics apps may stutter the first few runs after cleaning. No need to keep — one of the common large caches.

apps-common:nvidia-installer.what: Temp files left after driver installers unpack, plus old installer packages.
apps-common:nvidia-installer.advice: Cleaning does not affect installed drivers; rolling back a driver version needs the old package re-downloaded. No need to keep.

apps-common:amd-intel-shadercache.what: Shader caches generated by AMD and Intel GPU drivers.
apps-common:amd-intel-shadercache.advice: Graphics programs stutter slightly the first few runs after cleaning. No need to keep.

apps-common:vscode-cache.what: Extension caches, logs, and UI caches of VS Code.
apps-common:vscode-cache.advice: First launch after cleaning rebuilds caches and is slightly slower; extensions themselves are unaffected. No need to keep. Do not delete the neighboring User folder — that holds settings and keybindings.

apps-common:jetbrains-cache.what: Index caches, logs, and plug-in temp files of IDEA / PyCharm and other JetBrains IDEs.
apps-common:jetbrains-cache.advice: The first project open after cleaning spends a long time 'indexing' — large projects can take ten-plus minutes. Keep caches for very large projects, or use the IDE's Invalidate Caches instead.
apps-common:jetbrains-cache.tip: It rebuilds, but the whole project must be re-indexed first.

apps-common:adobe-media-cache.what: Preview and audio-waveform caches generated by Premiere / After Effects, often tens of GB.
apps-common:adobe-media-cache.advice: Reopening a project regenerates previews and waveforms, and the editor stutters for a while. Keep caches for projects in progress, or you wait on every open.
apps-common:adobe-media-cache.tip: It rebuilds, but previews must regenerate.

apps-common:davinci-cache.what: Optimized media and render caches generated by the editor.
apps-common:davinci-cache.advice: Playback and rendering regenerate caches after cleaning and are noticeably slower meanwhile. Keeping them suits projects in progress.

apps-common:blender-cache.what: Blender's temp render files, autosaves, and collage caches.
apps-common:blender-cache.advice: Cleaning also removes the autosave files used for crash recovery. Keep while rendering or working — autosaves sometimes rescue unsaved work.

apps-common:office-filecache.what: Local copies and upload caches Office keeps when saving documents; noticeable mainly with OneDrive.
apps-common:office-filecache.advice: If a local copy still holds changes not yet synced to the cloud, cleaning can lose those changes. Confirm all documents finished syncing before cleaning.

apps-common:onedrive.what: Local copies of cloud files and on-demand placeholder files.
apps-common:onedrive.advice: Deleting local copies does not delete the cloud files, but it scrambles sync state and may trigger a full re-sync. Keep them; to free space use the file's right-click 'Free up space'.

apps-common:baidu-netdisk.what: Download caches, thumbnails, and logs of the cloud-drive client.
apps-common:baidu-netdisk.advice: Cleaning also removes in-flight download chunks; unfinished downloads start over. Keep while download tasks are running.

apps-common:thunder-idm.what: Chunk temp files and metadata of download managers.
apps-common:thunder-idm.advice: Cleaning an unfinished task's temp files forces that task to re-download. Keep while tasks are unfinished.

apps-common:docker-desktop.what: Docker's images, containers, and volume data.
apps-common:docker-desktop.advice: Deletion loses all local images and container data, including un-exported database contents. Keep; slim down with docker system prune.

apps-common:wsl-vhdx.what: The virtual disk file of each WSL distro; the more you install, the bigger it gets.
apps-common:wsl-vhdx.advice: Deleting equals removing every file and configuration inside that Linux environment. Keep; to reclaim space, run docker system prune first and then compact the vhdx.

apps-common:windows-store-cache.what: Download and UI caches of the Microsoft Store.
apps-common:windows-store-cache.advice: After cleaning, rebuild with wsreset, otherwise Store pages may misload. No need to keep.

games-titles:the-witcher-3.what: Game files of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, including both large expansions.
games-titles:the-witcher-3.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling; progress saves usually live under Documents, not in this folder. Keep while you still want to play it.

games-titles:cyberpunk-2077.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling; saves live under Documents\CD Projekt Red and are not deleted with it. Keep while you still want to play it.

games-titles:gta-v.what: Game files of Grand Theft Auto V, including Online.
games-titles:gta-v.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling; Online character data lives on the servers and is unaffected. Keep while you still want to play it.

games-titles:rdr2.what: Game files of Red Dead Redemption 2.
games-titles:rdr2.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling. Keep while you still want to play it.

games-titles:elden-ring.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling; saves live under AppData\Roaming\EldenRing. Keep while you still want to play it.

games-titles:baldurs-gate-3.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling; saves live under AppData\Local\Larian Studios. Keep while you still want to play it.

games-titles:starfield.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling; mods and saves must be rebuilt as well. Keep while you still want to play it.

games-titles:hogwarts-legacy.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling. Keep while you still want to play it.

games-titles:cs2.what: Game files of Counter-Strike 2, still using the old CS:GO folder name.
games-titles:cs2.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling; about 30 GB must be re-downloaded. Keep while you still play it.

games-titles:dota2.what: Game files of Dota 2; the folder name still carries the beta suffix.
games-titles:dota2.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling. Keep while you still play it.

games-titles:pubg.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling. Keep while you still play it.

games-titles:apex.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling. Keep while you still play it.

games-titles:destiny2.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling. Keep while you still play it.

games-titles:mhw.what: Game files of Monster Hunter: World.
games-titles:mhw.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling; saves live in Steam Cloud or the local userdata folder. Keep while you still want to play it.

games-titles:mh-wilds.what: Game files of Monster Hunter Wilds.
games-titles:mh-wilds.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling. Keep while you still want to play it.

games-titles:sekiro.what: Game files of Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice.
games-titles:sekiro.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling. Keep while you still want to play it.

games-titles:dark-souls-3.what: Game files of Dark Souls III.
games-titles:dark-souls-3.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling. Keep while you still want to play it.

games-titles:terraria.what: Game files of Terraria; the install is small.
games-titles:terraria.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling; saves live under Documents\My Games\Terraria. Keep while you still want to play it.

games-titles:stardew-valley.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling; saves live under AppData\Roaming\StardewValley. Keep while you still want to play it.

games-titles:hollow-knight.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling. Keep while you still want to play it.

games-titles:hades.advice: Deleting equals uninstalling. Keep while you still want to play it.
